title: Inheritance and Virtual Functions
summary: Build class hierarchies, override behavior with virtual functions, and store different types behind base class pointers.
intro: Inheritance lets one class build on another, and virtual functions let code written for the base class run the right behavior for each derived class. You will derive classes, override methods, store mixed objects in one vector of `std::unique_ptr`, and see exactly when each constructor and destructor runs.

steps.title: Base and derived classes

example.title: A dog is an animal
example.prompt: Derive Dog from Animal, then call an inherited method and a new one.
example.output:
Animal Rex created
Dog Rex created
Rex is an animal
Rex fetches the ball
example.explanation: Building `rex` runs `Animal(name)` from the initializer list first, so `Animal Rex created` prints before the Dog constructor body. `describe()` is inherited: Dog never declares it, but a Dog can call it because it is public in Animal. `fetch()` is new in Dog and reads `name_` directly, which works because `name_` is protected. If it were private, only Animal's own methods could use it.

practice.title: A bike is a vehicle
practice.prompt:
Build a Bike on top of a Vehicle, then call an inherited method and a new one.

1. Read a bike name and a bell count.
2. Write `class Bike : public Vehicle` with a private `int bells_`.
3. Its constructor calls `Vehicle(name, 2)` in the initializer list, stores the bell count, then prints `Bike <name> created`.
4. Add a public `void ringBell() const`, which prints `<name> (<wheels> wheels):` followed by ` ring` once per bell, using the protected `name_` and `wheels_`.
5. In `main`, create the Bike, then call `info()` and `ringBell()`.

Input:

```text
Comet 3
```

Expected output:

```text
Vehicle Comet created
Bike Comet created
Comet has 2 wheels
Comet (2 wheels): ring ring ring
```

tests.output:
Vehicle Comet created
Bike Comet created
Comet has 2 wheels
Comet (2 wheels): ring ring ring

Vehicle Zip created
Bike Zip created
Zip has 2 wheels
Zip (2 wheels): ring

Vehicle Bolt created
Bike Bolt created
Bolt has 2 wheels
Bolt (2 wheels):

hints: Start the class with `class Bike : public Vehicle {` and put the constructor under `public:`.
The initializer list is `: Vehicle(name, 2), bells_(bells)`. The base must come first.
Print the prefix once, then loop `bells_` times printing `" ring"`, then print `'\n'`.

steps.title: Virtual functions and override

example.title: Reporting shapes
example.prompt: Override virtual functions in Circle and Square and print each shape through a base class reference.
example.explanation: `report` only knows it has a `const Shape&`, yet each call runs the right `name()` and `area()` because both are virtual and the derived classes override them. The `Shape*` pointing at the square dispatches the same way. `copy` is a real Shape object built from only the Shape part of the circle, so the radius is gone and the base versions print `shape 0.00`. That is slicing, and it is why polymorphic objects are passed by reference or pointer.

practice.title: Payroll
practice.prompt:
Compute pay for two kinds of employees through one base class reference.

1. Read an hourly employee as `name hours rate`, then a salaried employee as `name salary`.
2. In `Hourly`, override `pay()` to return hours times rate and `role()` to return `hourly`.
3. In `Salaried`, override `pay()` to return the salary and `role()` to return `salaried`.
4. Create both employees and call the given `printPay` on the hourly one, then the salaried one. It prints the name, the role, and the pay with 2 decimals, separated by spaces.
5. Point a `const Employee*` at the salaried employee and print `pointer: ` followed by its `role()`.

Input:

```text
Ana 40 15.50
Ben 3000
```

Expected output:

```text
Ana hourly 620.00
Ben salaried 3000.00
pointer: salaried
```

tests.output:
Ana hourly 620.00
Ben salaried 3000.00
pointer: salaried

Cy hourly 227.50
Dee salaried 2750.75
pointer: salaried

Eve hourly 0.00
Fin salaried 1500.00
pointer: salaried

hints: Copy the base signature exactly and add `override`: `double pay() const override { ... }`.
If a line prints `employee 0.00`, your override is missing or its signature does not match.
Point the `const Employee*` at the salaried object with `&`, then call `role()` through `->`, just like `p` in the example.

steps.title: Abstract classes and polymorphic containers
steps.body:
Often the base class has no sensible default. Write `= 0` to make a function *pure virtual*:

```cpp
virtual double area() const = 0;
```

A class with at least one pure virtual function is *abstract*. `Shape s;` does not compile, because a Shape alone has no area. A derived class becomes concrete once it overrides every pure virtual function.

To hold different shapes in one container, store pointers, since a `std::vector<Shape>` would slice (and cannot even hold an abstract type). Use `std::unique_ptr` so the vector owns each object:

```cpp
std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>(1.0));
```

`std::make_unique<Circle>` returns a `std::unique_ptr<Circle>`, which converts automatically to `std::unique_ptr<Shape>`. Each object lives on the heap and the vector holds 8 byte pointers to them. Loop with `for (const auto& s : shapes)` and call through `s->`. A `const auto&` matters here: copying a unique_ptr does not compile.

`push_back` moves the temporary unique_ptr into the vector, so only a pointer changes hands. That is also why the declared virtual destructor, which turns off the implicit moves from the copy and move lesson, costs nothing here: the objects themselves stay put on the heap.

example.title: Total area
example.prompt: Store circles and rectangles behind an abstract Shape and print each area and the total.
example.explanation: Shape is abstract, so the program can only create Circles and Rectangles. Each `std::make_unique` result converts to `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` as it is pushed. The loop sees only Shape pointers, and `s->area()` dispatches to the real class of each object. When `main` returns, the vector is destroyed, each unique_ptr deletes its shape, and the virtual destructor makes sure the derived part is cleaned up too.

practice.title: Monthly fees
practice.prompt:
Store different account types in one vector and add up their monthly fees.

1. In `Basic`, override `monthlyFee()` to return 2.00 plus 0.50 per transaction and `kind()` to return `basic`.
2. In `Premium`, override `monthlyFee()` to return 12.00 and `kind()` to return `premium`.
3. Read `n`, then `n` lines of `type owner transactions`, and push a `Basic` or `Premium` into `accounts` with `std::make_unique`.
4. For each account print the owner, the kind, and the fee, separated by spaces.
5. Print `total ` followed by the sum of all fees. Every number has 2 decimals.

Input:

```text
3
basic Ana 6
premium Ben 40
basic Cy 0
```

Expected output:

```text
Ana basic 5.00
Ben premium 12.00
Cy basic 2.00
total 19.00
```

tests.stdin:
3
basic Ana 6
premium Ben 40
basic Cy 0
tests.output:
Ana basic 5.00
Ben premium 12.00
Cy basic 2.00
total 19.00

hints: Copy each signature from Account, drop the `= 0`, and add `override`.
`transactions_` is protected, so `Basic::monthlyFee()` can read it directly. Choose the class to create with `if (type == "basic")`.

Fill the vector with `std::make_unique<Basic>(...)` or `std::make_unique<Premium>(...)`, then loop with `for (const auto& a : accounts)` as in the example. With zero accounts only the total line prints.

steps.title: Virtual destructors and destruction order

example.title: Watching objects die
example.prompt: Store two Derived objects as base class pointers and print every constructor and destructor call.
example.explanation: Each `std::make_unique<Derived>` builds the Base part first, then the Derived part. The loop pops the back element, so Derived 2 dies before Derived 1. Each pop destroys a `std::unique_ptr<Base>`, which deletes through a `Base*`. Because `~Base` is virtual, `~Derived` runs first and `~Base` follows. The vector is empty before `done`, so nothing is left for its destructor and the order is fully under your control.

practice.title: Buttons on a panel
practice.prompt:
Create a row of buttons and show the full construction and destruction order.

1. Read `n`, the number of buttons.
2. Write `class Button : public Widget`. Its constructor calls `Widget(id)` and prints `Button <id>`. Its destructor prints `~Button <id>` and is marked `override`.
3. Push buttons with ids 1 to `n` into `widgets` as `std::unique_ptr<Widget>`.
4. Empty `widgets` with a `pop_back` loop, then print `done`.

Input:

```text
3
```

Expected output:

```text
Widget 1
Button 1
Widget 2
Button 2
Widget 3
Button 3
~Button 3
~Widget 3
~Button 2
~Widget 2
~Button 1
~Widget 1
done
```

tests.output:
Widget 1
Button 1
Widget 2
Button 2
Widget 3
Button 3
~Button 3
~Widget 3
~Button 2
~Widget 2
~Button 1
~Widget 1
done

hints: The constructor is `explicit Button(int id) : Widget(id) { ... }`, and `id_` is protected, so Button can print it.
Write the destructor as `~Button() override { ... }`. It runs before `~Widget` automatically.
Push with `std::make_unique<Button>(id)` in a loop from 1 to `n`, then reuse the example's `while (!...empty())` loop.

recap:
- `class Derived : public Base` makes Derived a kind of Base. Base's public members stay public, and `protected` members are the ones Derived can use but outside code cannot.
- Call the base constructor in the initializer list. The base is built first and destroyed last.
- `virtual` plus `override` lets a call through `Base&` or `Base*` run the derived version. Without `virtual`, the base version runs.
- Copying a derived object into a `Base` by value slices it, so pass by reference or pointer.
- `= 0` makes a function pure virtual and the class abstract, so it cannot be created on its own.
- `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>>` holds mixed objects, filled with `std::make_unique<Derived>(...)`.
- Every class with virtual functions needs a virtual destructor so deleting through a base pointer runs `~Derived` then `~Base`.
- A `pop_back` loop destroys elements last in, first out. The vector's own destruction order is unspecified.
